phonemes.desc: Long stressed [ɑː] plus voiced alveolar lateral [l] and voiceless labiodental [f]; álfr means 'elf'
Diphthong [ɛi̯] — a rising glide from open-mid to close front, the standard Old Norse ei sound
Bilabial nasal [m] plus tapped or trilled [r]; final -r is the masculine nominative ending

pronunciation.approximation: 'AHLV-haymr' — stress the first syllable like 'owl' without the w, then a quick 'lv-haymer' with a rolled final r.

kin.label: Old English
kin.form: ælf, 'elf' — the same Germanic word as Old Norse álfr, as in the compound ælfscíene, 'elf-beautiful'

kin.label: German
kin.form: Alptraum, literally 'elf-dream', a distant echo of elf-influenced sleep

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: álfar, the light elves themselves, fairer than the sun to look upon

pronunciation.note: Old Norse á is a long back vowel, and ei is a diphthong; the acute accent on Á marks stress and length together. The form Álfheimr is Tier 1 because it preserves the acute accent on Á — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: Realm of the Light Elves
domains.subtitle: The domain of Álfheimr
domains.lead: In the Norse cosmology recorded by Snorri Sturluson, Álfheimr is the bright home of the ljósálfar, the light elves — 'fairer than the sun to look upon' — one of the worlds layered into the structure of the universe. The gods gave the realm to Freyr as a tooth-gift, binding the Vanir god of fertility to an elven people, and its fair folk glide along the border between the divine order and the luminous Otherworld that later Scandinavian folklore knew as the land of the huldufólk.

cards.name: Light Elves
cards.desc: The álfar of Álfheimr are said to be fairer than the sun to look upon, associated with fertility and subtle natural power.

cards.name: Freyr's Inheritance
cards.desc: The gods gave Álfheimr to Freyr when he cut his first tooth, binding the Vanir god to the elven realm.

cards.name: Alvíssmál Catalogue
cards.desc: The dwarf Alvíss records the elves' own names for sun, moon, and earth, testifying to Álfheimr's distinct voice.

cards.name: Luminous Otherworld
cards.desc: Later folklore merged the light elves with landvættir and huldufólk, a radiant realm bordering every farm.

mythology.lead: Álfheimr enters the record as a gift, a place-name, and a people. The eddic poems and Snorri's prose agree that the light elves hold a realm of their own, ruled by Freyr; beyond that the sources grow deliberately blurry, and scholars still argue whether the 'dark elves' are dwarfs, death-folk, or a tidying invention of Snorri's Christian-era system. The realm's mythology is mostly threshold lore: what stands at the bright edge of the human world, and what it asks of us.

myths.title: The Tooth-Gift of the Gods
myths.text: The fullest account of the gift is a single half-stanza. Grímnismál 5 runs: 'Álfheim the gods gave to Freyr in days of old, as a tooth-gift (tannfé)' — the customary present to an infant when the first tooth appears — and Snorri repeats the line in his enumeration of the heavenly regions (Gylfaginning, ch. 8, Faulkes trans.). The infant gift becomes a sovereign realm: Freyr, the Vanir hostage-guest among the Aesir, is made lord of a distinct cosmic territory with a people of its own. The detail marks Álfheimr within the Vanir sphere — the same god who dispenses sun and rain over the fields also governs the elven homeland — and it hints at an older stratum of belief in which elves were not minor spirits but a nation among the nations of the cosmos, with standing enough to be granted by divine assembly.

myths.title: The Dwarf's Catalogue
myths.text: Alvíssmál, 'The Sayings of All-Wise,' is structured around a journey from under the earth to the world above. The dwarf Alvíss seeks to marry Þórr's daughter, and the thunder-god delays him through the night by asking what things are called among the different peoples. Alvíss names the same objects — earth, heaven, moon, sun, cloud, wind, sea, fire, forest, night, and seed — according to the speech of gods, men, giants, and elves (Alvíssmál sts. 9–35). The elves' vocabulary is one of the catalogues: testimony to the Norse sense that Álfheimr possessed its own idiom and its own way of naming the world. When dawn breaks and turns the dwarf to stone, the poem also confirms the old idea that sunlight is fatal to creatures of the dark — while the light elves dwell in its radiance. The catalogue is the myth: a world is real to the Norse imagination when it has its own words for common things.

myths.title: Fairer than the Sun
myths.text: Listing the regions of heaven for King Gylfi, Snorri's informant Hár says: 'That which is called Álfheim is one, where the people live that are called light-elves; but dark-elves live down in the earth, and they are unlike them in appearance, and much more unlike them in nature. Light elves are fairer than the sun to look upon, but dark elves are blacker than pitch' (Gylfaginning, ch. 8, Faulkes trans.). It is the closest thing the tradition gives us to a description of Álfheimr, and it is framed as a comparison — the realm defined by its inhabitants' beauty, set against a shadowed twin below. Scholars have long debated what Snorri meant by the pairing: a genuine old duality, an echo of the dökkálfar of later saga conflated with dwarfs, or the systematizing hand of a Christian antiquary arranging his cosmos like a catechism (see Gunnell, 'How Elvish Were the Álfar?'). The disagreement itself is the point: Álfheimr glows most brightly precisely at the edge of definition.

myths.title: The Álfablót
myths.text: The firmest witness to the cult of the elves is not an eddic poem but a traveler's inconvenience. Around 1018, Sigvatr Þórðarson journeyed through Sweden on King Óláfr's business and was turned away from a farmhouse where the household was keeping the álfablót — the sacrifice to the elves. The housewife at the door refused him entry, saying that she feared Óðinn's wrath, for they were holding the elven sacrifice (Sigvatr Þórðarson, Austrfararvísur sts. 4–6, ed. Whaley). The poet complains of the rebuff in mocking verses, but the incidental detail is gold: a century after Iceland's nominal conversion, elves were still receiving blood-offerings behind closed doors, and the rite was serious enough to bar a king's man. Álfheimr, in other words, was not only poetic geography — it was worshipped territory, with a festival the neighbours respected and a boundary the uninvited could not cross.

lore.syncretism: Álfheimr's afterlife is a study in survival through renaming. As Christianity took hold, the álfar were never formally condemned — they slipped sideways into the folklore of the landvættir and, in Iceland, the huldufólk, the 'hidden people', whose dwellings were respected into the modern age; later saga tradition muddled Snorri's dark elves with dwarfs until the categories nearly merged. The nineteenth-century folklore collectors restored the record — Jón Árnason's Íslenzkar þjóðsögur (1862–64) gathered the elf-legends of Iceland wholesale — and the Romantic movement made the elf a symbol of national landscape. The twentieth century returned the name to its Eddic glory: Tolkien, who lectured on Völuspá and said his elves owed much to the álfar of the Elder Edda, built Quenya and Sindarin around the word. Modern Heathenry has revived the álfablót itself. Through every transformation the pattern holds: the luminous realm migrates, but it never vanishes.
lore.culturalLegacy: Álfheimr today lives a double life. In Iceland, belief-adjacent respect for the huldufólk remains culturally legible — road projects have been rerouted around suspected elf-rocks, and the hidden people still surface in polls and news copy as a way of talking about the land's claims. In modern Heathen and neopagan practice, the álfablót has been reconstructed as a festival of the elves and ancestors. And the realm has conquered global fantasy: Tolkien's debt to the Eddas is explicit, and Álfheimr — under its own name — recurs in comics, games, and novels as the stock 'elf-world' of Norse-flavored cosmologies. The Unicode restoration of the name is a small act of precision in that traffic: Álfheimr is not a generic fairyland but a specific medieval Scandinavian idea of where the beautiful neighbors live.
lore.extendedMeditation: Álfheimr is the geography of the near-neighbor. Every culture has an Otherworld, but the Norse one is strikingly local: not a heaven far overhead but a bright country just past the ridge, close enough that a housewife can turn a poet away from its festival. The elf-home condenses a whole theory of how the world is furnished — that nature is populated, that beauty is political, that the boundary of the farm is also the boundary of the human. To restore the acute accent on Á is to mark the name as Old Norse and not generic; but the deeper restoration is the reminder that Álfheimr was once part of a working cosmology, with sacrifices, taboos, and neighbours. We have flattened the elves into mascots. The Eddas remember them as a nation.

sources.name: Poetic Edda: Grímnismál 5 (Álfheim given to Freyr as tannfé); Alvíssmál 9–35 (the elves' names for the world); trans. Carolyne Larrington (Oxford, 2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda: Gylfaginning ch. 8 (the light and dark elves of Álfheim), trans. Anthony Faulkes (Everyman, 1987).
Sigvatr Þórðarson, Austrfarvísur sts. 4–6 (the álfablót), in Diana Whaley (ed.), Poetry from the Kings' Sagas 1 (Skaldic Poetry of the Scandinavian Middle Ages I, 2012).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford, 2001), s.v. elves.
Gunnell, Terry, 'How Elvish Were the Álfar?' in The Nordic Storyteller: Essays in Honour of Knut Liestøl (Costerus New Series, 2007).

lore.archaeology: No artifact bears the label 'Álfheimr'; the realm's material traces are indirect. The documentary bedrock is the skaldic stanza — Sigvatr's account of an álfablót performed around 1018 — which establishes the cult a century and more after conversion. Onomastics preserves the footprint: Álf- compound farm and place-names in Norway and Iceland (álfhóll, 'elf-hill', is a recurring element) mark remembered elf-territory. The high-status boat burials of Oseberg (c. 834 CE) and Gokstad preserve the aristocratic culture in which álfar beliefs circulated, and small finds — amulets and figurines variously read as valkyries, gods, or landvættir — show the population of the spirit world, though none can be pinned to the light elves specifically. The most persistent 'site' is folkloric: elf-hows, elf-stones, and elf-fields catalogued by nineteenth-century collectors, still pointed out in Scandinavian and Icelandic landscapes.
